summary.en: Prepare the inspection so the right work is checked against the right requirements at the right time.

whenToUse.en: Before planned work, before a defined inspection point, or whenever upcoming work may become concealed or difficult to verify later.

detail.en: Identify the activity, location, lot/area and stage of work to be inspected.
Check current drawings, specifications, approved submittals, ITP/PIE/PRIE, procedures and applicable acceptance criteria.
Confirm hold, witness, surveillance and testing points and required notifications.
Verify preceding work, approvals, materials, access, equipment and test readiness.
Align with superintendent/foreman, subcontractor, testing agency and owner/consultant as required.
Have checklist, measuring tools, camera, drawings and forms ready.
Arrive early enough to observe the condition before it is covered or altered.

keyReminders.en: Plan from the work sequence, not only from the calendar.
A good inspection starts before arriving at the workface.
If a critical point may be missed, communicate early.

commonMistakes.en: Inspecting after concealment
Using an old drawing revision
Arriving without knowing acceptance criteria
Failing to coordinate third-party or owner witness requirements

summary.en: Establish what 'acceptable' means before inspecting or making a quality decision.

whenToUse.en: Before inspection, testing, acceptance, deficiency/NCR issuance, material verification, or whenever requirements appear conflicting or unclear.

detail.en: Define the exact component, system, location and activity.
Locate contract drawings/specifications and applicable approved procedures.
Verify the document is approved/current for construction.
Review approved submittals, shop drawings, RFIs, changes, manufacturer instructions and ITP criteria.
Do not invent an interpretation; identify discrepancies and obtain clarification through the approved channel.
Convert the requirement into observable or measurable checks.
Keep the document/revision reference supporting the inspection decision.

keyReminders.en: Verify the requirement first; do not inspect from memory when the requirement is available.
A manufacturer instruction does not automatically override the contract hierarchy.
If documents conflict, escalate through the project's defined authority chain.

commonMistakes.en: Judging from personal preference
Using superseded drawings
Quoting a requirement without its revision/context
Treating an unresolved conflict as a field decision

summary.en: Use the approved inspection/test plan to control inspection sequence, responsibilities, intervention points and records.

whenToUse.en: When an activity is governed by an ITP, PIE, PRIE or equivalent inspection/testing plan.

detail.en: Confirm activity, scope and revision.
Know who performs, verifies, witnesses and accepts each point.
Ensure preceding stages and required approvals are complete.
Do not pass a hold point without required release; provide witness notice as required.
Complete inspections and tests against listed criteria.
Enter objective results, references, evidence and signatures/approvals as required.
Route deficiencies or non-conformities through the defined process.
Ensure all required stages are signed/closed and traceable.

whatToCapture.en: Linked test reports, photos, NCRs or deficiencies

keyReminders.en: The ITP is a control map, not merely a form to sign at the end.
A missed hold point can invalidate downstream assurance.
Use the project's definitions for H/W/S/R points.

commonMistakes.en: Back-filling signatures
Skipping points because the work looks acceptable
Treating witness and hold points as interchangeable
Failing to link supporting records

summary.en: Control critical inspection stages so required parties can verify work before it proceeds.

whenToUse.en: When the ITP/quality plan or contract defines hold, witness, review or surveillance points.

detail.en: Confirm type, requirement, responsible party and notification period.
Ensure work and prerequisite documentation are ready for inspection.
Issue notice using the approved communication method and lead time.
For a hold point, do not proceed until formal release is obtained.
Record observations, results and evidence.
Capture required acceptance, waiver or authorized release.
Link the release to the activity, location and inspection record.

keyReminders.en: Hold point = stop until authorized release, unless the governing procedure expressly provides otherwise.
Witness-point rules can vary; follow the project's notification and waiver procedure.
Never self-release a point outside your authority.

commonMistakes.en: Proceeding because the inspector did not arrive
Verbal release with no record when formal release is required
Late notification
Confusing surveillance with hold/witness requirements

summary.en: Verify completed or in-progress work against defined requirements and record an objective result.

whenToUse.en: At planned inspection stages, before concealment, at completion of an activity, or when acceptance is required.

detail.en: Verify scope, location and current requirements.
Inspect condition, installation, workmanship and interfaces.
Use suitable calibrated/verified tools where measurement is required.
Determine compliance against explicit requirements.
Capture results, measurements, photos and references.
Accept, identify deficiency, initiate NCR, or seek clarification according to project rules.
Notify responsible parties and record required approvals.
Link the inspection to location, activity and supporting records.

keyReminders.en: Acceptance must be based on requirements, not appearance alone.
Record actual values when a measurable criterion exists.
Do not sign for work you did not inspect unless the procedure explicitly permits record-based verification.

commonMistakes.en: 'Looks good' without criteria
Recording only pass/fail with no evidence for critical checks
Accepting concealed work that was not verified
Using uncalibrated equipment where calibration is required

summary.en: Record an observed quality issue that requires correction but is handled below the project's formal NCR threshold.

whenToUse.en: When work has a correctable issue and the project quality plan permits it to be managed as a deficiency/punch item rather than an NCR.

detail.en: State what is wrong and where.
Confirm the expected condition.
Capture objective description, location and photos/measurements.
Confirm the issue belongs in the deficiency process rather than NCR or RFI.
Assign/communicate through the approved process.
Responsible party completes correction.
Verify the corrected condition.
Record verification and closure evidence.

keyReminders.en: A deficiency is not a way to avoid an NCR when the NCR criteria are met.
Describe the condition, not the person who caused it.
Closure requires verification.

commonMistakes.en: Vague descriptions such as 'fix wall'
No location reference
Closing from a contractor's message without verification
Using deficiency and NCR terminology interchangeably

summary.en: Control, document and resolve work, material or installation that does not conform to an applicable requirement.

whenToUse.en: When the project's NCR criteria are met: a specified requirement is not satisfied and formal control/disposition is required.

detail.en: Determine exactly what does not comply and where.
Confirm the applicable drawing, specification, approved submittal, procedure, code or other governing requirement.
Prevent concealment, continuation, use or incorporation of affected work where required.
Record location, element ID, condition, photos, measurements and requirement.
Follow the project's NCR communication and quality procedure.
Use authorized disposition such as rework, repair, replace, reject, or accept-as-is/concession where formally permitted.
Ensure the approved disposition/action is completed.
Confirm the resulting work satisfies the approved disposition and applicable requirements.
Record verification, evidence, approvals and formal closure.

keyReminders.en: Do not close the NCR merely because the repair was performed; verify the completed work first.
Do not prescribe an engineering disposition unless you have the authority to do so.
Keep the original non-conforming condition traceable to its final disposition.
If accept-as-is/use-as-is is proposed, obtain the approval required by the contract and quality procedure.

commonMistakes.en: Writing the NCR before confirming the requirement
Blaming individuals instead of describing facts
Allowing affected work to be concealed
Using 'repair' and 'rework' casually where the project distinguishes them
Closing without disposition approval or verification

items.en: Terminology, disposition authority, stop-work/containment requirements and NCR thresholds vary by organization and contract. Follow the approved project quality plan.

summary.en: Implement and verify action that removes the cause or condition associated with a quality problem and prevents or reduces recurrence where required.

whenToUse.en: When an NCR, repeated deficiency, audit finding, trend, test failure or other quality event requires formal corrective action.

detail.en: State the issue and scope using evidence.
Control affected work/material where necessary.
Use an appropriate root-cause method proportional to significance.
Specify what will correct the condition and, where required, address recurrence.
Make ownership and timing explicit.
Complete approved actions and retain evidence.
Check that the action worked, not merely that it was performed.
Document verification and approval.

keyReminders.en: Correction fixes a detected condition; corrective action may address why it occurred. Follow project terminology.
Root-cause depth should match risk/significance.
Effectiveness verification may require observing later work, not only reviewing a completed form.

commonMistakes.en: Calling every repair a root-cause corrective action
Choosing a cause without evidence
Closing immediately after implementation
Actions with no owner or due date

summary.en: Confirm that corrected, repaired, reworked or otherwise dispositioned work now satisfies the required condition.

whenToUse.en: After deficiency correction, NCR disposition, failed inspection/test, or corrective work requiring verification.

detail.en: Understand the requirement, condition and approved disposition.
Ensure the work is ready for verification.
Verify the correction itself and relevant interfaces.
Use the same acceptance basis or approved revised basis.
Determine whether closure criteria are met.
Capture results, photos, measurements and linked records.
Close only if acceptable; otherwise keep open/escalate.

keyReminders.en: Reinspection is an independent verification step, not an administrative checkbox.
Verify the whole affected condition where the correction could create secondary issues.
Maintain linkage to the original record.

commonMistakes.en: Checking only that work was attempted
Closing without viewing inaccessible corrected work
Creating a new unrelated record with no link to the original

summary.en: Create objective, retrievable evidence that shows what was inspected, where, when and against what requirement.

whenToUse.en: During inspections, tests, receiving, deficiencies/NCRs, corrective work, concealed-work verification and closeout.

detail.en: Know the condition/result the evidence needs to support.
Take an overview establishing location/orientation.
Photograph the specific feature, defect, measurement or identification.
Use measuring device, tag, gridline or element identifier without obscuring the condition.
Link date, location, activity and record ID.
Describe what the image demonstrates.
Place evidence in the approved system and connect it to the relevant record.

keyReminders.en: A photo without context may prove very little.
Capture evidence before concealment or correction when possible.
Do not rely on photos alone when a measurement/test record is required.
Follow project privacy/security rules when people, sensitive assets or restricted information may appear.

commonMistakes.en: Only close-up photos with no location context
Blurry or dark images
No caption or record linkage
Photographing a tape measure at an unreadable angle
Using edited images that obscure original evidence

summary.en: Plan, witness, record and evaluate required quality tests using approved methods and traceable results.

whenToUse.en: When specifications, codes, ITPs or procedures require testing of materials, systems or completed work.

detail.en: Identify method, frequency, sample/location and acceptance criteria.
Confirm test area/material, equipment and prerequisites.
Check qualified personnel/laboratory and calibration/certification where required.
Assign traceable sample, location or equipment identification.
Follow approved method and record actual results.
Compare against acceptance criteria.
Notify and initiate required deficiency/NCR/retest process.
Link signed report and supporting evidence to the work.

keyReminders.en: Record actual test values, not just 'pass'.
A retest does not erase the original failed result.
Confirm sampling frequency and location requirements before work advances.

commonMistakes.en: Missing sample location
No calibration traceability
Discarding failed results after a passing retest
Using wrong units or acceptance criteria

summary.en: Verify delivered materials/equipment are correct, approved, undamaged and traceable before incorporation into the work.

whenToUse.en: At delivery, before storage/use, and before installation where receiving verification is required.

detail.en: Confirm purchase/submittal/material description and intended use.
Check approved submittal/product data and required certifications.
Look for damage, contamination, deterioration or improper packaging.
Check manufacturer, model/type, grade, size, heat/batch/lot numbers where applicable.
Confirm delivery ticket, certificates, test reports and compliance documents.
Protect material from damage or environmental exposure.
Apply project controls to nonconforming or unverified material.
Link material to delivery, lot and installation area where required.

keyReminders.en: Approved product does not mean every delivered unit is automatically acceptable.
Preserve identification needed for later traceability.
Quarantine unverified/nonconforming material according to project procedure.

commonMistakes.en: Material installed before approval
Certificates filed without linking them to delivered lots
Damaged material accepted because product type is correct
Losing batch/heat identification

summary.en: Obtain an authorized clarification when contract information is missing, conflicting, ambiguous or unsuitable for a reliable field decision.

whenToUse.en: When the inspector cannot determine the requirement without interpretation or when documents conflict.

detail.en: State the exact technical issue and location.
Check drawings, specifications, submittals, prior RFIs and changes first.
Reference the affected documents and revisions.
Identify work affected, timing or quality risk without overstating.
Use the project's RFI/clarification process.
Do not treat informal discussion as final where formal response is required.
Ensure the authorized response is reflected in the work and records.
Connect response to inspection/change/as-built documentation.

keyReminders.en: Ask a focused question; do not write an RFI that hides the actual conflict.
An RFI is not automatically authorization to change scope, cost or design.
Use the response only within the authority and scope stated.

commonMistakes.en: Submitting before checking available documents
Suggesting an unapproved design solution as if accepted
Proceeding on a verbal answer when formal response is required
Failing to link the response to affected inspections

summary.en: Ensure field decisions and inspections use the latest authorized information and that changes remain traceable.

whenToUse.en: When drawings, specifications, RFIs, site instructions, change notices, shop drawings or procedures are revised.

detail.en: Confirm source, status and approval.
Determine systems, locations, inspections and records impacted.
Prevent unintended field use according to document-control procedure.
Ensure relevant teams have access.
Update inspection criteria, ITPs/checklists or pending inspections where needed.
Check work reflects the authorized revision.
Maintain traceability between old/new documents and affected records.

keyReminders.en: 'Latest file received' is not always 'approved for construction.' Verify status.
Never erase revision history needed to explain earlier inspections.
Revisit completed or ongoing work if a revision has retrospective impact.

commonMistakes.en: Inspecting from a superseded drawing
Deleting old records rather than superseding them
Assuming an RFI response is a formal drawing revision
No impact review for work already installed

summary.en: Maintain a defensible chain connecting the installed work to requirements, materials, inspections, tests, issues, approvals and closeout records.

whenToUse.en: Throughout construction, especially for critical materials, concealed work, testing, NCRs and turnover documentation.

detail.en: Know what identifiers and links the project requires.
Use location, lot, batch, heat, serial, inspection or record IDs.
Connect materials, certificates, submittals and requirements.
Connect inspections, tests, photos and ITP points.
Maintain NCR/deficiency/corrective-action linkage.
Keep the document basis used at the time of inspection.
Check the chain can be followed without relying on memory.
Organize records for turnover/retention.

keyReminders.en: A record is traceable only if another person can follow the chain later.
Use consistent identifiers across systems.
Do not depend on filenames alone where metadata/record IDs are available.

commonMistakes.en: Photos not linked to an activity
Certificates with no installed-location linkage
NCR closure detached from original inspection
Renaming files in ways that break references

summary.en: Confirm required quality obligations are complete, verified, organized and ready for turnover.

whenToUse.en: At system, area, milestone or project completion and before final quality turnover.

detail.en: Review contract, quality plan and turnover checklist.
Confirm required records are complete and accepted.
Close or formally disposition deficiencies, NCRs and corrective actions.
Complete final inspections/punch verification as required.
Organize ITPs, inspection reports, test reports, certificates, approvals and evidence.
Confirm records can be linked to systems/areas/assets.
Ensure final/as-built/O&M/commissioning interfaces are coordinated where within QC scope.
Obtain required reviews, approvals and retention/hand-off.

keyReminders.en: Closeout begins during construction, not at the end.
Do not hide unresolved items to make the dossier appear complete.
Verify completeness and retrievability, not merely file count.

commonMistakes.en: Waiting until project end to organize records
Missing signatures/revisions
Open NCRs buried in turnover files
Duplicate/uncontrolled records with unclear final status
